[Teaching & Learning](../../teaching.qmd) / Elementary Statistics

::: {.course-introduction}

<span class="course-eyebrow">Sample course design</span>

Statistics provides ways to describe patterns in data, investigate questions, and draw appropriately cautious conclusions. Materials in this collection will include short explanations, worked examples, practice questions, and demonstrations that let learners explore how statistical ideas work.

This sequence draws from my **proposed Elementary Statistics (PSYC 210) sample syllabus for Cerritos College**. It is **not an assigned, approved, or currently running course**. The institution's approved course outline would determine final content, materials, and requirements.

:::

## Learning pathway

The proposed 18-week syllabus is organized here into seven units. The week labels refer to the sample syllabus, not scheduled course dates. All 16 interactive learning resources for Weeks 2–18 are available for instructional review. The eight resources for Weeks 9–18 are marked as working drafts; all materials may be revised.

[Start the interactive learning pathway](lessons/sampling-bias.qmd). Each lesson includes links to the previous and next resource and back to this overview.

::: {.course-module}
::: {.course-module__number}

01

:::
::: {.course-module__body}

### Research questions and descriptive statistics

<span class="course-module__weeks">Weeks 1 to 4</span>

Populations and samples; observational and experimental research; variables, measurement, sampling, and bias; frequency distributions and graphs; center, variability, standard deviation, z-scores, outliers, and introductory scatterplots.

**Week 2 interactive lesson:** Compare random, restricted convenience, and stratified sampling to explore sampling variability and bias.

[Explore Sampling Methods and Bias](lessons/sampling-bias.qmd)

**Weeks 3–4 interactive lesson:** Compare distribution shapes, manipulate an observation, and explore the mean, median, variability, and standardized scores.

[Explore Distributions, Center, and Variability](lessons/distributions-and-variability.qmd)

:::
:::

::: {.course-module}
::: {.course-module__number}

02

:::
::: {.course-module__body}

### Probability and sampling distributions

<span class="course-module__weeks">Weeks 5 to 6</span>

Basic and conditional probability, independence, normal distributions, sampling distributions, the central limit theorem, and standard error.

**Week 5 interactive prototype:** Explore how the area under a normal curve represents probability, then compare theoretical probabilities with repeated simulated observations.

[Explore Probability and the Normal Distribution](lessons/normal-probability.qmd)

**Week 5 interactive lesson:** Explore conditional probabilities, contingency tables, independence, and mutually exclusive events.

[Explore Conditional Probability and Independence](lessons/conditional-probability.qmd)

**Week 6 interactive lesson:** Draw repeated random samples, compare sample means, and investigate how sample size affects the variability and shape of the sampling distribution.

[Explore the sampling distributions lesson](lessons/sampling-distributions.qmd)

:::
:::

::: {.course-module}
::: {.course-module__number}

03

:::
::: {.course-module__body}

### Estimation and statistical inference

<span class="course-module__weeks">Weeks 7 to 8</span>

Point estimates, confidence intervals, precision, hypothesis testing, p-values, Type I and Type II errors, effect size, and introductory statistical power.

**Week 7 interactive lesson:** Construct repeated confidence intervals and explore coverage, precision, and uncertainty.

[Explore Confidence Intervals and Coverage](lessons/confidence-intervals.qmd)

**Week 8 interactive lesson:** Explore the null distribution, two-sided p-values, and statistical decisions through repeated sampling.

[Explore Hypothesis Testing and P-values](lessons/hypothesis-testing.qmd)

**Week 8 interactive lesson:** Investigate Type I and Type II errors, statistical power, and the influence of sample size, variability, and effect size.

[Explore Statistical Power and Decision Errors](lessons/statistical-power.qmd)

:::
:::

::: {.course-module}
::: {.course-module__number}

04

:::
::: {.course-module__body}

### Comparing means

<span class="course-module__weeks">Weeks 9 to 12</span>

The Week 9 midterm covers Weeks 1 to 8. Instruction then moves to the t-distribution and one-sample t-test, followed by independent-samples and paired-samples t-tests, one-way ANOVA, assumptions, and selected nonparametric alternatives.

**Weeks 9–10 interactive lesson (working draft):** Compare Student’s t and normal distributions, one-sample, independent-samples, and paired-samples t-tests.

[Explore The t-Distribution and Comparing Means](lessons/t-tests.qmd)

**Week 11 interactive lesson (working draft):** Explore between-group and within-group variability, the F-statistic, and effect size.

[Explore One-Way ANOVA](lessons/anova.qmd)

**Week 12 interactive lesson (working draft):** Examine unusual observations, assumptions, and sensitivity to analysis choices.

[Explore Assumptions and Analysis Sensitivity](lessons/assumptions.qmd)

:::
:::

::: {.course-module}
::: {.course-module__number}

05

:::
::: {.course-module__body}

### Categorical data analysis

<span class="course-module__weeks">Week 13</span>

Chi-square goodness-of-fit and independence tests, observed and expected counts, and categorical association.

**Week 13 interactive lesson (working draft):** Compare observed and expected counts in goodness-of-fit and independence tests.

[Explore Chi-Square Tests](lessons/chi-square.qmd)

:::
:::

::: {.course-module}
::: {.course-module__number}

06

:::
::: {.course-module__body}

### Correlation and regression

<span class="course-module__weeks">Weeks 14 to 15</span>

Correlation, direction and strength, outliers, restricted range, confounding and causation; simple linear regression, slopes, residuals, prediction, and limits of extrapolation.

**Week 14 interactive lesson (working draft):** Investigate direction, strength, outliers, and restricted range in scatterplots.

[Explore Correlation and Scatterplots](lessons/correlation.qmd)

**Week 15 interactive lesson (working draft):** Fit a regression line, examine residuals, and explore prediction and extrapolation.

[Explore Simple Linear Regression](lessons/regression.qmd)

:::
:::

::: {.course-module}
::: {.course-module__number}

07

:::
::: {.course-module__body}

### Applying and communicating statistics

<span class="course-module__weeks">Weeks 16 to 18</span>

Week 16 focuses on integrating methods, analysis selection, effect size, power, practical importance, and preliminary project results. Week 17 covers communicating findings, project presentations, and cumulative review. The cumulative final examination occurs in Week 18.

**Week 16 interactive lesson (working draft):** Choose an analytical method for applied research scenarios and explain why it fits.

[Explore Choosing a Statistical Method](lessons/method-selection.qmd)

**Weeks 17–18 interactive lesson (working draft):** Interpret results, communicate uncertainty and limitations, and practice cumulative statistical reasoning.

[Explore Communicating Results and Cumulative Review](lessons/interpretation-review.qmd)

:::
:::

## Laboratory and applied project

The sample syllabus proposes **eight graded laboratory reports**, alongside guided practice and project development. The Week 6 sampling distributions activity supports **Lab 3**, which asks students to simulate sampling variability and examine the effect of sample size. The interactive lesson is practice material, not a graded laboratory submission.

The proposed software approach uses free tools: R with instructor-provided scripts and guidance, or potentially jamovi, depending on departmental preferences. Prior programming experience is not assumed.

Project milestones in the sample syllabus are a research question and dataset proposal in **Week 5**, a preliminary analysis plan in **Week 12**, a revised analysis plan and preliminary results in **Week 16**, and a final submission and brief presentation or accessible equivalent in **Week 17**.

For the project, students would use an instructor-approved public, de-identified, or simulated dataset and explain their research question, descriptive results, analysis choices, assumptions, practical importance, and limitations. Collecting sensitive personal information is not required.

## Learning materials and accessibility

The sample syllabus identifies the freely available [OpenStax *Introductory Statistics 2e*](https://openstax.org/details/books/introductory-statistics-2e) as a potential textbook.

Browser-based activities will include explanatory text, keyboard-operable controls, and accessible alternatives as appropriate. Course announcements, graded assessments, and student records would remain in Canvas.
